course.title: Atomic – Cambridge Lower Secondary Science — Stage 8

unit.title: Diet and Growth
unit.blurb: The nutrients in food and their jobs, balancing energy in and out, what a balanced diet looks like, and the habits that help or harm growth and health.

O1.t: Identify the nutrients in a balanced diet and the job of each, including vitamins A, C and D, calcium and iron, water and fibre.

O2.t: Explain why we need food, and that carbohydrates and fats are the body's main energy stores.

O3.t: Balance energy in and energy out, describe a balanced diet and explain the effects of malnutrition.

O4.t: Discuss how sleep, exercise, alcohol, smoking and vaping affect growth and health, and how food choices affect the environment.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was written by the Atomic teaching team to
help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence.
Let's begin!
Welcome to Stage 8, Unit 1: Diet and Growth.
The nutrients in our food are like building blocks.
They build strong bones and muscles, fuel our brains for learning,
and keep our bodies working.
What nutrients do we need, and which habits help us stay healthy?
Let's find out.
Our bodies need nutrients for energy, as building materials,
and to control body processes.
We get them from food.
Carbohydrates give us energy, proteins are needed for growth and repair,
and fats and oils store energy.
Vitamins help the body work correctly,
and minerals help the body grow and work properly.
We also need water and fibre.
They aren't nutrients, but they're essential.
Water is a major part of blood and is needed for the body's chemical reactions.
Fibre keeps the digestive system healthy.
A drop of orange-brown iodine solution is put on bread, sugar,
potato and cheese. Iodine turns blue-black if starch is present.
Predict: which foods will turn blue-black?
Pause and decide.
Watch. One drop of iodine solution goes onto each food.
The bread and the potato turn blue-black.
The sugar and the cheese stay orange-brown.
Explain what you saw.
Bread and potato are starchy foods:
starch is a complex carbohydrate that plants store.
Sugar is a carbohydrate too, but it is not starch,
so iodine stays orange.
Cheese is mostly protein and fat, so it has no starch.
Pause and explain it in your own words.
Carbohydrates are like fuel for a car: they give us energy for walking,
running and even thinking.
Starch is a complex carbohydrate and our main source of energy.
It's found in bread, rice, pasta, oats, potatoes and corn.
Sugars, found in sweets, sugary drinks, honey and syrup,
are absorbed into the blood quickly, giving fast energy.
But refined sugars contain no other nutrients,
and extra carbohydrates are turned into fat and stored in the body.
Fibre is also a carbohydrate, found in fruit, vegetables, whole grains,
nuts and seeds. We can't digest it, so it's not a nutrient.
But it helps us feel full, adds bulk to undigested food,
moves waste through the gut, prevents constipation and slows down sugar absorption.
Proteins help the body repair damaged cells and make new ones.
They're also needed to make enzymes and hormones.
Proteins come from meat, fish, eggs, cheese, nuts and milk.
Vegetarians and vegans can get them from plants such as peas and beans.
Fats and oils help us absorb some vitamins, build parts of cells,
protect our organs and keep us warm.
Plant fats, like nuts and olive oil, are healthier than animal fats.
Fats and oils have more than double the energy value of carbohydrates,
so most of our stored energy is fat.
That's how a hibernating bear survives winter!
The liver also stores a little carbohydrate, called glycogen.
Only when carbohydrates and fats run out does the body use protein,
breaking down muscle. So we need a balance of all nutrients.
We need only small amounts of vitamins, but each has its own job.
Vitamin A, from carrots, spinach and pumpkin,
keeps eyes and skin healthy and helps fight infection.
Without enough, you may struggle to see in dim light and get ill more often.
Vitamin C, from oranges, strawberries and papayas, keeps gums healthy,
helps cuts heal and helps us absorb iron.
A lack causes bleeding gums and slow healing.
Vitamin D helps us absorb calcium for strong bones and teeth.
Our skin makes it in sunlight, and we get it from eggs,
mushrooms and sardines. A lack causes weak bones.
But be careful: too much of some vitamins can be harmful too.
We need minerals in small amounts too.
Calcium, from milk, yoghurt, cheese and green vegetables,
builds strong bones and teeth and helps muscles and nerves work.
Iron, from meat, liver, eggs and leafy greens, is needed to make haemoglobin,
which carries oxygen in red blood cells.
Too little iron makes us tired and weak.
Our cells are mostly water,
and every chemical reaction in the body needs it.
We lose water when we sweat, urinate and breathe out,
so we should drink about 1.5 to 2 litres,
roughly six to eight glasses, every day,
and more on hot days or when exercising.
Food labels use these standard values for the energy in one gram of each nutrient.
Carbohydrate and protein both give about 17 kilojoules per gram.
Fat gives 37: more than double.
Fibre gives only about 8.
Pause and decide: which gives more energy,
10 grams of fat or 10 grams of carbohydrate, and how much more?

captions: The energy in food is measured in kilojoules or kilocalories,
and it's shown on food labels.
To keep a healthy body mass,
we need to balance the energy we take in from food
with the energy we use in activity and body processes.
Take in more than you use, and the extra is stored as fat.
But not everyone needs the same amount.
Energy needs depend on age, sex, how active you are, and individual differences.
Growing children need plenty of calcium and protein for bones and muscles,
while older adults may need more vitamin D and fibre.
A balanced diet contains a variety of foods,
giving us all the nutrients we need.
Healthy eating plates show that half of our plate should be fruit and vegetables.
A quarter should be starchy foods, especially wholegrain ones,
which also give us fibre, and a quarter should be protein.
Choose healthier oils, drink water rather than sugary drinks, and stay active.
Malnutrition means not getting the right amounts of nutrients,
either too little or too much.
A severe lack of protein causes a disease called kwashiorkor.
Taking in much more energy than we use, over a long time,
can lead to obesity, which raises the risk of heart disease,
high blood pressure and a type of diabetes.
Eating too little leaves the body weak and tired.
A balanced lunch gives a mix of nutrients.
Here is one lunch box, item by item.
A wholegrain sandwich gives starch for energy,
and fibre to keep the gut healthy.
The egg filling gives protein,
which the body uses for growth and to repair cells.
Carrot sticks give vitamin A, and an orange gives vitamin C,
plus minerals and fibre.
A bottle of water instead of a sugary drink keeps you hydrated without extra sugar.
Pause and decide: a friend's lunch is crisps, chocolate and a fizzy drink.
Which nutrients are missing?

captions: Staying healthy isn't just about food.
Our lifestyle matters too.
Getting about 8 hours of good-quality sleep helps you
feel rested and helps your brain work better.
Regular exercise makes the heart, lungs, muscles and bones stronger.
It reduces stress, lifts your mood,
helps you sleep and stops you getting ill so easily.
Running and jumping strengthen the heart, and lifting weights builds muscle strength.
Always warm up, start slowly and cool down afterwards.
Stretching and yoga make joints and muscles flexible.
Together with a balanced diet,
exercise helps the body keep a healthy balance of muscle, bone and fat.
A student starts exercising for 30 minutes, five times a week,
and measures her resting heart rate every two weeks.
At the start her resting heart rate is 78 beats per minute.
After eight weeks it has fallen to 69.
Regular exercise makes the heart muscle stronger,
so it pumps more blood with each beat.
Pause and decide: why does a stronger heart need fewer beats per minute at rest?
Some habits harm our growth and health.
Eating lots of foods high in sugar,
salt and certain fats can cause tiredness, poor concentration, weight gain,
diabetes and heart disease.
A lack of protein,
calcium and vitamin D can stunt growth and weaken bones.
Alcohol can harm the brain and lead to addiction.
If a pregnant woman drinks alcohol,
it can damage her baby's brain and slow its growth.
Smoking and vaping are very harmful.
Tobacco smoke contains nicotine,
which is addictive and raises heart rate and blood pressure; carbon monoxide,
which stops the blood carrying oxygen; and tar,
which coats the lungs and increases the risk of lung cancer.
Smoke harms people nearby too, and can slow children's growth.
Can our diet be more sustainable?
Cattle release carbon dioxide and methane, which are greenhouse gases.
As demand for meat grows,
more land is needed for grazing and animal feed,
which can lead to deforestation.
Food scientists now make plant-based burgers that look and taste like meat,
using rice flour, beans, vegetables and beet juice for colour.
Pea protein contains all the essential building blocks of proteins,
and one company adds soy leghaemoglobin,
which is similar to the iron compounds in meat.
Eating more plant-based food can help the environment,
as long as our diet still gives us all the nutrients we need.
